analysis.evidence: תֶרַח is the subject of וַיְחִי, “he lived,” and remains the subject of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered.” The three sons are each introduced by אֶת.
analysis.morphology: Personal proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 66828:2, 66584:5.
analysis.morphology: Cardinal numeral, common gender, plural absolute.

analysis.evidence: וַיְחִי תֶרַח שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה means “Terah lived seventy years.” The singular שָׁנָה follows שִׁבְעִים (“seventy”) and gives the unit of Terah’s age.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute common noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיּוֹלֶד אֶת אַבְרָם, אֶת marks Abram as the first direct object of וַיּוֹלֶד ‘he fathered’. The particle recurs before Nahor and Haran, the other two sons named.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Clear the unsupported root אבה and its link to article 2bh. Preserve the explanation of the compound name and its recorded bearer.
draft.definition: Abram, the earlier name of Abraham, son of Terah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 identifies Abram as Terah’s son, and Genesis 17:5 records his change of name. The first element of אַבְרָם is the noun אָב, “father.” Neither verse supports deriving the name from אָבָה, “be willing.”

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered.” The repeated אֶת marks Abram, Nahor and Haran as his sons. Genesis 17:5 identifies Abram as the man whom God renames Abraham.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew masculine singular personal name with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אֶת is a separate word.
analysis.sense: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: In אֶת נָחוֹר, אֶת marks Nahor as the second of the three named sons who serve as direct objects of וַיּוֹלֶד ‘he fathered’.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Terah’s son as a second bearer of the name alongside Serug’s son.
draft.definition: Nahor is the personal name borne here by Terah’s son, Abram’s brother and Milcah’s husband.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 lists Abram and Nahor among Terah’s sons. Genesis 11:29 names Milcah as Nahor’s wife.

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of וַיּוֹלֶד (“he fathered”). The repeated אֶת marks Abram, Nahor, and Haran as its objects, identifying this Nahor as Terah’s son and Abram’s brother.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אֶת is a separate direct-object marker.
analysis.sense: Nahor, Abram’s brother and Milcah’s husband

draft.definition: Introduces a definite direct object, here a person identified by name.
draft.evidence: In Gen.11.26, וְאֶת הָרָן marks Haran as the third named object of וַיּוֹלֶד.

analysis.evidence: Terah fathered אֶת אַבְרָם אֶת נָחוֹר וְאֶת הָרָן. Each son’s name has its own object marker, and וְ joins Haran to Abram and Nahor as the last son named.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וְ means “and.” אֶת is the unsuffixed direct-object particle before the name הָרָן.
analysis.sense: Marks Haran as a definite direct object of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered.”

evidence.note: וְאֶת הָרָן closes the list of sons whom Terah fathered.

article.name: הָרָן
article.summary: Genesis 11:26 names Haran among Terah’s sons, alongside Abram and Nahor. The origin of the name is uncertain.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for הָרָן with the root unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 names Haran as the third son listed after “he fathered.” The verse gives no etymology for his name.

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered.” Each son’s name has its own object marker in אֶת אַבְרָם אֶת נָחוֹר וְאֶת הָרָן, identifying Haran as a son alongside Abram and Nahor.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name in a single segment. The preceding וְאֶת is a separate word that marks the name as the final coordinated direct object of וַיּוֹלֶד.
